yarn.meaning: Every ingredient, quantity, temperature, time and storage note survives. Additions hang off the original: "(call it 220°C)" converts the given temperature, "or it'll turn out tough as old boots" explains the overmixing warning, "(good luck with that)" reacts to leftovers.
yarn.sense: Terms mostly fit: "knock up", "bung it in the oven", "whack it in", "Keep your mitts off it", "tea towel". "(supper, if you're posh about it)" misreads the original's "dinner (supper)" gloss; in Australia supper is a late snack, not a posh word for the evening meal.
yarn.authenticity: Sounds like an Aussie cook talking: "Crank the oven up", "give the pan or tin a good spray", "dish it up", "gettin' stuck in", "don't knock it till you've tried it".
yarn.register: A full level-4 kitchen yarn that still works as a recipe, with swearing at dad level: "some buggers".
yarn.tone: The friendly how-to tone survives and the steps stay clear, but a couple of asides tip into mild mockery of the dish: "Sounds a bit weird, I reckon".
yarn.flow: Reads naturally aloud: "Tip the batter into the pan and whack it in the oven."
yarn.variety: Wide range with no tic: "knock up", "feed", "brekkie", "bung", "whack", "tough as old boots", "mitts", "chuck".
yarn.essence: Still clearly the Wikibooks Southern Cornbread recipe, with its structure (intro, ingredients, equipment, procedure, notes) intact.

engine.meaning: Nearly all content survives as the original, but "lunch or tea (tea)" garbles the dinner/supper gloss into a meaningless repetition.
engine.sense: "tea" for dinner fits, but the doubled "(tea)" loses the sense; "some buggers" is an odd fit for people who eat cornbread in buttermilk.
engine.authenticity: US recipe text left in place ("self-rising corn meal", "whole milk", "skillet") with filler bolted on: "Now, beat egg in the bowl", "Well, Pour the batter".
engine.register: Almost entirely untranslated; a few insertions ("Now,", "Well,", "some buggers") are all that changes in a level-4 brief.
engine.tone: The neutral recipe tone mostly survives because the text is untouched; "some buggers" adds an odd sneer.
engine.flow: Broken joins: "Well, Pour the batter into the skillet", "lunch or tea (tea)", "Now, beat egg in the bowl."
engine.variety: A couple of fillers ("Now," twice, "Well,") and one swear word; nothing to vary.
engine.essence: Recognisably the original recipe, since it is mostly the original.

unharnessed.meaning: All quantities, steps and notes survive accurately: "Let it cool for 5 minutes in the pan before you serve it up", "kept in the fridge for a few days".
unharnessed.sense: Terms fit: "self-raising", "full-cream milk", "frypan", "baking tin", "lunch or dinner (tea, if you like)", "give it a spray of non-stick".
unharnessed.authenticity: Natural Australian kitchen talk: "Crank the oven up", "bung it in", "getting stuck into it", "don't overmix the bugger". "a doddle" is a Britishism.
unharnessed.register: Clearly Aussie and dad-level, but a notch lighter than level 4: headings and some lines stay close to the source ("Notes, tips, and variations", "Medium or large mixing bowl").
unharnessed.tone: Keeps the friendly, practical recipe voice without mocking the dish.
unharnessed.flow: Smooth throughout: "Stir in the cornmeal and mix till it's just wet through. The batter'll be a bit lumpy."
unharnessed.variety: Good range ("doddle", "dished up", "knock together", "brekkie", "bung", "whack"), though "frypan" recurs in nearly every step.
unharnessed.essence: Plainly the same recipe, in the same structure.

yarn.why: Turns the original's regional gloss into a class joke; Australians would not hear "supper" as the posh word for the evening meal.

yarn.quote: Sounds a bit weird, I reckon
yarn.original: by crumbling cornbread into a glass of buttermilk and eating it
yarn.why: An aside that passes judgement on the dish, which the neutral original does not.

yarn.quote: That's it. That's the whole shopping list.
yarn.why: Added filler; harmless colour, but it pads the ingredients section.

engine.why: The gloss is now a repetition that says nothing.
A filler stuck before a capitalised imperative; broken grammar.
A swear word dropped in without a voice around it; it reads as a sneer.

engine.quote: 2 cups yellow or white self-rising corn meal
engine.original: 2 cups yellow or white self-rising corn meal
engine.why: US terms and forms left throughout (self-rising, whole milk, skillet); the text is barely translated.

unharnessed.why: "doddle" is British more than Australian; "dead easy" or "a cinch" would sound more local.

summaries.yarn: A lively, natural level-4 recipe yarn that keeps every detail, adds a handy Celsius conversion and only harmless colour. One gloss is slightly mistranslated.
summaries.engine: The original with a few fillers and one swear word inserted, plus a garbled gloss. Far below the level-4 brief.
summaries.unharnessed: Accurate, natural and smooth, a little lighter than level 4. Very little to fault.
